messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prison Guard
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Media / News: Related news, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Hopelessness: I have no future, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo Alvarez is a 28-year-old prison guard who came to treatment months after the sudden death of his younger brother, who was killed in a car crash late at night while driving home alone. Mateo had been the person in the family everyone called steady and protective, and in the days after the death he became fixated on the fact that his brother had called earlier that evening and Mateo had not picked up because he was on shift. He returns to that detail again and again. In his mind, if he had answered, if he had kept him talking, if he had insisted he wait until morning, his brother might still be alive. What has settled in most deeply is not only grief but a harsh conviction that he failed at the one thing he was supposed to do: protect the people he loves.

Since the death, reminders of loss have become difficult to tolerate in ways that feel immediate and bodily. At work, the prison break room television often runs local news, and when a segment mentions a fatal crash or a family speaking about someone they have lost, Mateo feels the room go strangely far away. He describes a detached, unreal sensation, as if he is still standing there but not fully inside himself. In those moments he pulls his hands over his face, partly to block out the screen and partly to hide what is happening to him from other officers. He has also begun steering away from almost anything that reminds him of his brother or of bereavement more broadly, changing the channel, walking out when coworkers start talking about somebody’s funeral, refusing family conversations that turn toward memories. When he cannot get away cleanly, he sometimes picks an argument instead—snapping over minor things, escalating with his wife or a coworker—because anger feels more manageable than that sliding, unreal feeling.

These moments do more than upset him; they confirm the conclusions he has drawn about himself. Hearing stories about other people losing loved ones or feeling that sudden detachment can bring back, with full force, the belief that he is a man who did not protect his brother and that whatever used to be hopeful or light in him is gone for good. He says he used to be a happy person and now feels miserable almost all the time. The future, when he imagines it at all, looks flat and empty. That conviction follows him into ordinary settings. During intake he described standing in the prison corridor after hearing an inmate mention his dead mother during a phone call, and immediately thinking, not just of his brother, but of himself as someone marked by failure and with nothing ahead except more of the same.

Over time, those beliefs have begun shaping what catches his attention. Because he has come to expect pain and see himself through this lens of failed protection and permanent misery, talk of loss jumps out at him everywhere. The news in the staff room, a passing conversation about a death in another officer’s family, even the first hint of feeling unreal in his own body all register as signs that he is not okay and may never be okay. He listens for them without meaning to. The world has narrowed around themes of death and absence.

His ways of coping have made that narrowing worse. Avoiding grief reminders has left him increasingly cut off from his wife and extended family; he leaves the room when they want to talk about his brother, and afterward he takes his withdrawal as proof that happiness and closeness are over for him. Covering his face at work spares him a few moments of exposure, but it also reinforces his sense that these reactions are dangerous and shameful, something that must be hidden. The arguments he starts to distract himself bring brief relief, yet afterward he feels guilty, exhausted, and more convinced that he has become someone miserable to live with. Each of these habits seems to deepen the same bleak appraisal: that he failed, that he has changed permanently, that there is no real future to recover into.

They also leave him more easily thrown the next time something brushes against loss. Because he avoids reminders, even a short news clip can hit him with greater force. Because conflict has become one of the few ways he knows to escape the ache, tension at home and on the job keeps him keyed toward the next upsetting exchange. Because he hides his face and waits for the detached feeling to pass, the feeling itself has become a trigger he dreads and notices immediately.

Mateo sought help after his wife told him she no longer recognized him and after a recent shift in which a television report about a fatal accident left him frozen and unreal in the break room, hands over his face, before he picked a fight with a coworker who asked if he was all right. What frightens him most is that this is all that remains of him now: the brother who failed, the husband who brings home anger, the man with no future. What he hopes, cautiously, is not to forget his brother, but to be able to hear about loss without disappearing inside it.
